49: reference in the style library, `scripts/apply-design-md.cjs` derives the chart role

51: corpus gates, refuses to write on a failure, and places a hash-bearing provenance comment in both
52: theme blocks. Site extraction remains the job of `sk-design-md-generator`; this packet applies the
53: reference it receives.

91: granularity or reformats a label, and none of them may: a template never reads the clock,
92: and picking a format from the data is the analysis step that happens before the numbers
93: reach the file.

97: editing. The consequence is worth stating plainly, because it is easy to file as a
98: limitation: a chart of half-hourly readings needs labels already thinned and already
99: written the way they should appear. The form will not do it, and thinning rules in the
100: drawing code decide which of those labels are drawn, never what they say.
101: 
102: Numbers are the other way round. Every value in a data block is a raw number, and the file
103: formats it. Grouping, decimal places and the dash that stands in for a reading nobody took

109:

111:

113: | --- | --- |
114: | comparison | Which of these is biggest, and how do two periods sit against each other |
115: | composition | How does a whole divide up, or how do several independent measures stand |
116: | time | What happened over days, weeks or a year, how a period opened and closed, and how far along a target is |
117: | distribution | How are individual values spread |
118: | relationship | Do two variables move together, including across a run of periods, and how do a few entities compare across several measures |
119: | matrix | Which combinations of two discrete dimensions are hot |
120: 
121: ---
122: 
123: ## 5. THE NAME A READER ARRIVES WITH
124: 
125: A request almost never carries an id from the index. It carries the industry name for the picture, and the names in the table below appear nowhere in the index. The row ids say what a form draws, which is what makes them precise and also what makes them unfindable by searching for the word the reader used.
126: 
127: Every name in the left column already routes to this packet, so a request carrying one has arrived in the right place. A search that returns nothing is a naming mismatch rather than a missing capability. Read this table before reporting a gap.
128: 
129: | The reader says | Draw | What to know first |
130: | --- | --- | --- |
131: | heatmap, heat map | `heat-matrix` | The same chart under a different name. Two discrete dimensions, one cell per combination, shaded by value |
132: | calendar heatmap | `calendar-grid` | The same chart, fixed to one year of days with weekdays down and weeks across. A shaded matrix of anything other than days belongs in `heat-matrix` |
133: | donut chart | `unit-ring` | Same question, same ring, same total in the middle. The ring is built from countable ticks rather than from continuous arcs, which is the point: a reader counts marks instead of estimating angles. Parts that arrive as percentages rather than as whole-number counts belong in `unit-grid` |
134: | waffle chart | `unit-grid` | The same chart under a different name. One hundred squares, one per percent, filled in reading order |
135: | parallel coordinates | `parallel-axes` | The same chart under a different name. One vertical axis per dimension, one line per entity, every axis on its own scale |
136: | sparkline | `spark` | The same chart under its shorter name: one series, no axis, a trend at the size of a KPI row, read against itself. The latest value lives in the metric header, because the drawing itself prints no numbers |
137: | combo chart, dual axis chart, bar and line chart | `bar-line-composed` | The same chart under three names a reader is more likely to use than the row id. Columns for a count and a line for a rate over the same periods. The second scale is not a setting: the file draws one only when the two measures are an order of magnitude apart, and one ladder otherwise |

142: multi-dimensional answer and keeps both radar and arc-based pie out: mixed units do not become
143: honest by being normalised onto a polygon, and a reader can count the marks in `unit-grid` or
144: `unit-ring` instead of estimating an angle. That is a kept decision, not an unfinished gap.

152:

156: the reason it is absent.

181: ## 4. THE RULES
182: 
183: **One system per delivery.** A file, or a set of sibling charts shipped together, locks one system. When one chart in the set cannot be expressed in it, the whole set changes system or goes neutral. Recolouring the one exception is what makes a deck look assembled from parts. A `design-md` delivery is one such locked system: both palette blocks carry the same provenance and both clear the gates.
184: 
185: **Capacity is a ceiling, not a suggestion.** Four unordered categories is comfortable and five is not offered. A request for eleven categories is answered with the neutral system and labels, or by merging the tail before drawing. The ceiling lives in the palette file as the length of the series array, so an agent cannot reach a fifth slot without editing the source and failing the check.
186: 
187: **Derive light and dark, never introduce a hue.** A lighter value comes from mixing the chosen colour toward `surface`. A darker one comes from mixing it toward `ink`. Borrowing a value from another system to fill a gap breaks the encoding, because the borrowed value carries the other system's meaning. Every value shipped here was derived that way, inside one theme.
188: 
189: **A design-md delivery reads local values only.** `scripts/apply-design-md.cjs` parses the v3
190: `DESIGN.md` headings and columns, maps its background, text and chromatic rows into the shared
191: roles, and keeps the measured face before the substitute stack. It never fetches a site or copies a
192: remote resource. If the table cannot supply four chromatic values that clear the series gates, the
193: script names the shortfall and writes nothing.

239: marks with one that is.
240: 
241: **The emphasis is spent once per form.** It is the value that says which mark the sentence is
242: about, so a form that marks two marks has either two findings or no emphasis. It also has a size:
243: the marked mark tends to be the largest one, and two of them put more than half a figure's ink in
244: the colour reserved for the exception — which is the inversion above arriving by a different route.
245: When the sentence genuinely has two subjects, the repair is the sentence, not a second mark. The
246: `emphasis-budget` family holds it in both directions: more than one marked row fails, and a lead
247: rule in the styles that no row reaches fails too, because a colour defined and never painted is a
248: decision nobody made.
249: 
250: **A single-series Cartesian form starts on the first series token of its own system.** A line, bar
251: or area with one data stream uses `--chart-series-1` for its primary mark, whichever system the
252: form declares; a neutral form stays neutral rather than borrowing the categorical ramp, because the
253: categorical emphasis token is ink and the orange highlighted mark would be lost. The `--chart-emphasis` role remains for the one highlighted mark the headline is
254: about. This keeps a lone series inside the same series vocabulary that a multi-series form
255: will use later, while the emphasis still reads as a deliberate exception. Unit grids, rings,
256: ordered ramps and other non-Cartesian forms keep their existing colour logic; their colour is
257: encoding a part-to-whole, magnitude or structural question rather than a lone Cartesian stream.
258: 
259: The rule is the HTML corpus' projection of the frozen shadcn examples: line and area examples
260: paint through a named series token (`chart-line-default.tsx:68-73`, `chart-area-default.tsx:70-76`),
261: and custom dots reserve their separate treatment for an active or deliberately named point
262: (`chart-line-label-custom.tsx:87-97`).
263: 
264: **Shapes that touch are separated by a stroke in `surface`.** Stacked segments, pie slices and treemap cells all carry a surface-coloured separator, so no two data colours ever share an edge. This is what makes the contrast gate satisfiable: with the separator, every mark is read against the ground rather than against its neighbour. Without it, four categories on a light ground is arithmetically impossible, because all-pairs separation at 3:1 runs out of room after two values.
265: 
266: **Colour is never the only cue.** Categories keep labels, ordered data keeps position or length, emphasis keeps a headline. Remove the colour and the chart still has to be readable. That is an accessibility floor and it is also a hedge against a reader printing in greyscale.
267: 
268: **A single mark may sweep along its own ramp, and only where the system already encodes magnitude.** A sweep restates an ordering the data already has, which is why it is honest on an `ordered` system and dishonest anywhere else. On a `neutral` or a `categorical` series the same sweep invents an ordering the data does not have, so it is refused there. That permits it on `calendar-grid`, `heat-matrix` and `progress-single`, and forbids it on the other eighteen forms.
269: 
270: The rule is written to be testable rather than judged. A gradient whose stops name two different
271: series values is a sweep, and it may appear only in a file whose declared system is `ordered`. A
272: gradient whose stops name one series value at two opacities is a fade rather than a sweep, which
273: is what the area under the line in `daily-line` already is, and the rule leaves it alone.
274: 
275: Permission is not obligation, and two of the three permitted forms have nothing to sweep. A
276: calendar cell and a matrix cell each carry one value, so a gradient across one of them would
277: show a variation inside a single reading. Only `progress-single` draws a mark whose length is
278: the magnitude, so only `progress-single` carries the sweep. Its ramp is anchored to the whole
279: track rather than to the fill, which is what makes the shade at the bar's end mean how far along
280: the goal it is rather than simply the end of the bar. It runs from the fourth step to the first,
281: leaving out the step nearest the ground, because that step reads at 1.76:1 and a bar that starts
282: invisible against its own track is a bar that starts in the wrong place.
283: 
284: A gradient reference is not a colour and cannot be typed into a `fill`. It reaches the mark
285: through a custom property, the way every other value in a template does.
286: 
287: ---
288: 
289: ## 5. THE CONTRAST GATES
290: 
291: These are computed from the palette file on every run, never restated in a test. A test that copies the values goes stale the first time somebody edits a colour.
292: 
293: Every gate runs twice, once per theme, against that theme's own surface. A stock run prints the two
294: as separate lines, `palette-source` and `palette-source-dark`; a design-md run adds `design-md` lines
295: for each delivery block. Nobody reads one theme's pass as covering both. A value that clears on
296: paper has proved nothing about ink.
297: 
298: | Gate | Threshold | Applies to, on either ground |
299: | --- | --- | --- |
300: | `textOnSurface` | 4.5:1 | `ink` and `muted` against that theme's `surface` |
301: | `markOnSurface` | 3.0:1 | Every series value in an `importance` or `category` system, and every emphasis value |
302: | `rampDarkestOnSurface` | 3.0:1 | The step of a `magnitude` system furthest from the ground, which is the darkest on paper and the brightest on ink |
303: | `rampLightestOnSurface` | 1.15:1 | The step nearest the ground, so a low cell is distinguishable from an empty one |
304: | `rampStepSeparation` | 1.3:1 | Adjacent steps of a `magnitude` system |
305: | `emphasisAgainstFirstSeries` | 1.5:1 | Emphasis against `series-1` |
306: 
307: The design-md adapter applies `textOnSurface` to ink and muted, `markOnSurface` to all four series
308: and emphasis, and `emphasisAgainstFirstSeries` to emphasis; the corpus check then holds a delivery's
309: blocks to that set plus the series separation, comparing every pair of series rather than adjacent
310: values alone, with a pair passing on the ratio or on thirty degrees of hue. The two ramp-end gates
311: belong to the stock magnitude systems, and the adapter does not apply them. The rule role remains
312: deliberately ungated, but the dark rule still has to be the dark ink colour at a non-full alpha.
313: 
314: Two of those names were written when there was one ground and now read wrong on the other: on ink
315: the step this table calls the darkest is the brightest one. The check tests the end by its distance
316: from the ground rather than by its position in the array, and it says which end it tested in the
317: failure it prints.
318: 
319: The rename stays a proposal, and the reason has changed since it was first written. It is now a
320: scoping fact rather than a judgement: `rampDarkestOnSurface` and `rampLightestOnSurface` reach
321: three files, being this document, the palette source and the check that reads the keys by name,
322: and the check is the one file the phase that would rename them is not allowed to touch. Renaming
323: here and not there would leave a gate reading a key nobody defines, which is a worse state than
324: two badly named keys that work. `rampFarEndOnSurface` and `rampNearEndOnSurface` are the names
325: the rename should land under, and it lands as one edit across all three files or not at all.
326: 
327: ### Which end of a ramp the gates hold
328: 
329: A ramp's array runs from the value furthest from the ground to the value nearest it, and the check
330: asserts that ordering before it gates either end. That is what stops a reversed array from passing:
331: reversal keeps every step separation intact, so a check that gated whichever end happened to be
332: lighter would accept a ramp that now reads backwards.
333: 
334: ### Why a ramp is gated differently
335: 
336: A ramp step is read as part of a group, against its legend and its neighbours. An individual mark is read alone. Requiring 3:1 of every ramp step would delete the light end of every sequential scale, which is the half that encodes "low", so the gate holds the dark end and the step separation instead.
337: 
338: ### The one role deliberately not gated
339: 
340: `rule` is ungated, and this is a decision rather than an oversight. A gridline pushed to 3:1 competes with the data drawn over it, and it carries no information a reader has to recover. Structure that fails to read is a design defect reviewed by eye. The exemption is written into the palette file next to the gates so nobody has to guess whether it was intended.
341: 
342: ---
343: 
344: ## 6. WHAT IS ENFORCED AND WHAT IS NOT
345: 
346: Enforced by `scripts/check-corpus.cjs`, on every run:
347: 
348: - Every gate in the table above, computed from the palette file, once per theme against that theme's own surface. That holds for the three stock systems the palette file describes; the design-md adapter applies the subset named under the table, in `scripts/apply-design-md.cjs` at write time and again over a delivery's own blocks in the corpus check.
349: - Every system defines as many series values as its declared capacity, on both grounds.
350: - A `magnitude` system runs from the step furthest from the ground to the step nearest it, without reversing.
351: - The dark `rule` value is that theme's ink at an alpha, rather than a solid grey that a card edge would have to sit over.
352: - Each of a template's palette blocks matches the palette file exactly, in both directions, and no file carries more than one block per theme.
353: - A `design-md` block carries a first-line provenance comment with a well-formed 64-hex hash, and its inline values clear the same gates on both grounds.
354: - No colour literal appears anywhere outside a palette block.
355: - No corner value appears anywhere outside a palette block: a stylesheet corner resolves through a rung, and the drawing code computes a corner rather than typing one.
356: - An indexed data class carries the palette token of its own index, the indices run from one without a gap, and they stop at the declared system's capacity. `series-mapping` is the only rule that reads the mapping itself rather than the values on either side of it, and it is the rule a reversed or shuffled encoding fails. Everything else on this list passes a file whose classes hand the tokens out in the wrong order, because every other rule asks where a value came from and none asks which mark received it.
357: 
358: The sweep rule was the last entry on this list and it has moved up onto it. `gradient-sweep`
359: resolves each gradient's stops through the classes that carry them, counts the distinct series
360: values it finds and fails a gradient naming two of them in a file whose declared system is not
361: `ordered`. A gradient naming one series value at two opacities is a fade and is left alone,
362: which is what keeps the area under a line untouched.
363: 
364: Advisory, and reviewed by a person:
365: 
366: - Whether the gridline weight looks right at the size the chart ships.
367: - Whether two categorical hues that both clear the gate are still easy to tell apart. Their luminances are spread so the set survives greyscale, and that is a design property rather than a measurable one.
368: - Whether a sweep reads as one mark deepening rather than as two marks. That is the judgement the rule cannot make, and the reason the rule is a ceiling on where a sweep may appear rather than an instruction to use one.
369: 
370: The split is deliberate. A rule the tooling does not check describes the author's intentions rather than the artifact, so anything stated as binding above is checked, and anything that cannot be checked is named here as advice.
371: 
372: ---
373: 
374: ## 7. WHY THREE BUILT-IN SYSTEMS AND ONE ADAPTER
375: 
376: A fourth semantic system of "neutral with one accent colour" was considered and cut. Emphasis is a
377: role that every built-in system already carries, so a system whose only difference is that the role
378: is filled adds a name without adding an answer. In `neutral` the emphasis value is the only
379: chromatic colour in the palette, which is exactly what that fourth semantic system would have
380: delivered, reached by filling a role instead of by switching system.
381: 
382: `design-md` is not that system. It is an adapter for a measured local style reference: it changes
383: the values that fill the shared roles, records the source hash, and passes the same gates. It does
384: not add a new meaning to colour, a new capacity or a new chart form. The cost of keeping that
385: adapter separate is one more checker branch; the benefit is that stock source equality remains
386: strict and a themed delivery can be traced without putting client colours into the stock palette.
387: 
388: The emphasis role is required in all three built-in systems and in the adapter. A system where
389: emphasis is undefined has no way to express the most common request in the corpus: this one bar is
390: the point.
391: 
392: ---
393: 
394: ## 8. WHAT IS DELIBERATELY ABSENT
395: 
396: Two things a reader coming from a charting library will look for and not find. Both were
397: considered and both are cut, for the same reason section 7 cuts a fourth system: a name
398: that adds no answer costs more than the gap it fills.
399: 
400: ### A diverging system
401: 
402: A diverging ramp encodes distance from a meaningful midpoint, and it earns its place when a
403: form reads two directions away from zero on one continuous scale. No form in the corpus
404: does. `heat-matrix` and `calendar-grid` both run one direction from low to high, which is
405: what `ordered` already encodes, and `waterfall` separates rises from falls by category
406: rather than by magnitude, which is what `categorical` already encodes. Adding the system
407: now would mean shipping a scale with no consumer and letting an author reach for it because
408: it exists.
409: 
410: What would reopen it is a catalog form that genuinely needs a midpoint: a matrix of signed
411: change, a variance-against-plan grid, a correlation table. When such a form arrives, the
412: system arrives with it, and the two are added together so the scale has a consumer on the
413: day it ships.
414: 
415: ### Pattern fills
416: 
417: Hatching or dotting a mark so that colour is not the only cue is a real technique, and this
418: corpus does not need it. The rule above already forbids colour carrying meaning alone, and
419: every form satisfies it another way: a stacked segment carries its value in the segment, a
420: ring group carries its count beside the label, a scatter point carries a hover title, a band
421: carries a legend swatch in the same order as the stack. The luminances in each system are
422: spread so the set survives greyscale, which is the printing case patterns are usually
423: reached for.
424: 
425: The cost of adding them is not small. A pattern changes the visual register of every chart
426: it appears in, so it is either corpus-wide, which redraws the whole product for a problem
427: none of these forms has, or per-form, which makes two charts in one deck look like they came
428: from different tools. If a future form does encode something in colour alone and cannot
429: label it, that form carries the pattern, and this paragraph is the reason nothing else does.
430: 
431: ---
432: 
433: ## 9. RELATED DOCUMENTS
434: 
435: | Document | Purpose |
436: | --- | --- |
437: | [`template-contract.md`](./template-contract.md) | What a template file has to contain |
438: | [`catalog.md`](./catalog.md) | The index from a question to a chart form |
439: | [`../assets/style-reference/evilcharts/palettes.json`](../assets/style-reference/evilcharts/palettes.json) | The source of truth for every value |
440: | [`../scripts/README.md`](../scripts/README.md) | What the corpus check enforces |

13: ---
14: 
15: # Chart Colour Systems
16: 
17: Colour belongs to the Style Reference it was measured from. Every reference under
18: `assets/style-reference/` carries its own `palettes.json` beside its `DESIGN.md`, and the corpus
19: check fails a reference that carries none, so adding a reference is deciding its colour rather than
20: inheriting whichever palette happens to be the default.
21: 
22: What a reference owns is its colour, not the floors that colour has to clear. The contrast gates,
23: the type scale and the corner ladder are read from the default reference's file and apply to every
24: delivery, whichever reference painted it — a brand supplies values, it does not get to lower the bar
25: those values are measured against. A second reference's own `palettes.json` records the measurement
26: behind its values and is not read while that reference is not the default, which is why adding one is
27: a decision about colour and not about accessibility.
28: 
29: Every stock colour in this packet comes from the default reference's file,
30: `assets/style-reference/evilcharts/palettes.json`. A template never invents one, and the corpus
31: check fails a template that carries a colour literal anywhere except a palette block. A `design-md` delivery is the one request-time exception: its values come from a local v3
32: `DESIGN.md`, and the checker accepts them only by provenance plus the same inline gates.
33: 
34: Every role holds two values, one per ground. A file paints the light set by default and the dark set when the reader's operating system asks for one, and both sets come from the same file and clear the same gates.
35: 
36: ---
37: 
38: ## 1. OVERVIEW
39: 
40: Three built-in systems exist. A fourth identifier, `design-md`, is a request-time adapter for a
41: local v3 Style Reference rather than a fourth semantic encoding. Pick one built-in system per
42: stock delivery, or use the adapter with its provenance and gates.
43: 
44: ---
45: 
46: ## 2. THE QUESTION EACH SYSTEM ANSWERS
47: 
48: A colour system is an answer to "what does colour mean in this chart". That is the axis that
49: separates the three built-in systems. `design-md` answers a different question: which measured
50: local style reference should fill the same role vocabulary while the data encoding remains the
51: form's existing one.
52: 
53: | System | `encodes` | Colour encodes | Use it when | Capacity |
54: | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
55: | `neutral` | `importance` | Rank, by lightness alone. The series run from the value furthest from the ground: darkest first on paper, brightest first on ink | The default, and the fallback whenever hue would carry no stable meaning | 4 series |
56: | `ordered` | `magnitude` | Position on a scale | The data is ordered: a value, a rank, a time position, a progress figure | 5 steps |
57: | `categorical` | `category` | Category membership | The categories are unordered and there are four or fewer | 4 categories |
58: | `design-md` | `reference` | A measured local style mapped into the chart roles; the data still follows the form's declared encoding | The request names a v3 `DESIGN.md`, style reference or measured site's look | 4 series |
59: 
60: Start at `neutral`. Reach for another only when the data has the property that system encodes. A categorical palette on ordered data throws away the ordering, and an ordered ramp on unordered categories invents one. `design-md` is selected by the presence of the local reference, not by a new data meaning.
61: 
62: ### What the shadcn comparison kept
63: 
64: The shadcn comparison measured a much tighter categorical light-theme set than the standalone
65: one: shadcn light has a 16.0° minimum adjacent hue gap and 1.72:1 minimum own/opposite-ground
66: contrast, while standalone categorical light has a 92.9° gap and 3.37:1 minimum own/opposite-ground
67: contrast. The dark measurements were 71.1° and 2.92:1/2.15:1 for shadcn, against 96.5° and
68: 3.38:1/1.72:1 for standalone categorical. The numbers support keeping the standalone role split
69: and its existing gates rather than replacing it with a raw five-token ramp; they do not create a
70: new CVD or hue threshold here.
71: [SOURCE: specs/sk-design/018-sk-design-parent-v2/001-sk-create-chart/013-shadcn-reference-research/research/lineages/luna/research.md:55-66]
72: 
73: The transferable part is semantic indirection: a named series owns a palette token through its
74: key, and a mark reaches that token through the class the key declares. That keeps the palette
75: roles here while making a per-key colour change one auditable edit in the chart's series block.
76: [SOURCE: specs/sk-design/018-sk-design-parent-v2/001-sk-create-chart/013-shadcn-reference-research/research/lineages/luna/research.md:123-132]
77: 
78: ### Two names for one system
79: 
80: The second column exists because two vocabularies name these three built-in systems and both are
81: load-bearing. The id is what a file declares in its meta tag and what a catalog row carries. The
82: `encodes` value is a separate field in the palette source, and the contrast gates in section 5 and
83: the enforced list in section 6 are written against it rather than against the id, because what a
84: gate holds depends on what the colour means and not on what the system is called. They map one to
85: one, in the order above. A failure message quotes whichever of the two the rule it came from reads,
86: so the mapping is written here rather than inferred from a message.
87: 
88: `neutral` used to be described in this table as encoding nothing, which contradicted both the
89: palette source and the rest of its own row. Lightness is colour, and ranking by it is what
90: `importance` names.
91: 
92: ### How to settle a row against this table
93: 
94: The catalog carries a system per row, and that cell is a mirror of what the template declares
95: rather than a second opinion. So a row and a definition can disagree with nobody noticing, which
96: is what happened for as long as no one read the two documents against each other. The procedure
97: below is what a reader applies to settle one row, and it is written down so the answer is a
98: reading rather than a preference.
99: 
100: 1. **Name what colour is doing in that file.** Not what the chart is about. What the colour
101:    varies with. If it varies with nothing, the answer is already `neutral`.
102: 2. **Test the data for the property, not the chart for the vibe.** `categorical` needs
103:    categories that are unordered. `ordered` needs a position on a scale. A pair of periods and a
104:    before-and-after both have an order, and an order is what `categorical` does not have.
105: 
106:    A signed step looks like it belongs on that list and does not, and both sign-coloured forms in
107:    the corpus turn on the difference. `waterfall` and `candlestick` each draw a plainly ordered
108:    sequence, and in both the order is carried by position on the axis while colour varies with the
109:    sign alone: up or down, two classes with no rank between them. Step 1 settles it. The question
110:    is what colour varies with, not whether the data has an order somewhere in it, and on that
111:    reading both forms declare `categorical` correctly. Section 8 says the same thing from the
112:    other side, where it explains why the corpus has no diverging system.
113: 
114:    This step used to list a signed step among the ordered cases, which put it in direct
115:    disagreement with section 8 about the same two files.
116: 3. **`neutral` is the default and the fallback, so it wins a tie.** Leave it only when the data
117:    plainly has the property another system encodes. `neutral` carrying four series is not a
118:    workaround. Its capacity is four precisely so a form can draw several series and rank them by
119:    lightness, and a key printed beside those series is the ranking made legible rather than
120:    evidence that colour has started encoding membership.
121: 4. **Record an ambiguous row instead of resolving it.** Where the reading genuinely goes both
122:    ways, the row keeps the system it has and the ambiguity is written down. A row flipped on
123:    preference is how a corpus acquires a system nobody can defend.
124: 
125: ---
126: 
127: ## 3. THE ROLE VOCABULARY
128: 
129: A template reads a role, never a value. Every system defines the same roles, so the same markup renders under any of them.
130: 
131: ### Chrome roles, identical in all four identifiers
132: 
133: | Role | Custom property | What it is |
134: | --- | --- | --- |
135: | surface | `--chart-surface` | The page and card ground. Every ratio below is measured against it |
136: | ink | `--chart-ink` | Primary text: the headline, and any label read exactly |
137: | muted | `--chart-muted` | Secondary text: the subtitle, the axis labels, the source line |
138: | rule | `--chart-rule` | Gridlines, axis lines, card borders. Structure, never data |
139: 
140: Each of these carries a second value under `chromeDark`, chosen against the dark ground rather than
141: copied from the light one. The dark surface is the light theme's near-black taken one step deeper,
142: the dark ink and muted values are set to hold the ratio their light counterparts hold against paper,
143: and the dark rule is ink at an alpha rather than a solid grey, so a card edge sits on the ground
144: instead of drawing a second line over the data.
145: 
146: ### Corner roles, identical in all four identifiers
147: 
148: Not colours, and in the palette source they sit in their own object for that reason. They are
149: listed here because they are the other half of the role vocabulary a template reads: one 2px knob,
150: five steps, each earned by a surface the corpus actually draws.
151: 
152: | Role | Custom property | What it is |
153: | --- | --- | --- |
154: | mark | `--chart-radius-mark` | A data mark's corner: a bar end, a box body, a calendar cell, a legend swatch, a ring tick |
155: | track | `--chart-radius-track` | A percentage bar and the track it runs inside |
156: | swatch | `--chart-radius-swatch` | A colour block large enough to read as a panel rather than as a mark |
157: | pill | `--chart-radius-pill` | A progress track and its fill, which read as one capsule |
158: | card | `--chart-radius-card` | The card that holds the chart |
159: 
160: A corner computed from a mark's own geometry is not a rung. A range bar rounded to half its own
161: width is a lozenge, which is a shape rather than a shared value, and it stays in the drawing code.
162: 
163: ### Data roles, which are what a system changes
164: 
165: | Role | Custom property | What it is |
166: | --- | --- | --- |
167: | series | `--chart-series-1` upward | The data values in order. What the order means comes from the system |
168: | emphasis | `--chart-emphasis` | One value, for the single mark the headline is about |
169: 
170: ### What varies and what does not
171: 
172: In the three stock systems only the series values and the emphasis value change. A `design-md`
173: delivery also maps the chrome, typeface and corner ladder from its reference, but it keeps the same
174: role names and the same chart structure. That is what makes a themed chart still read as one
175: product rather than as a fourth rendering contract.
176: 
177: A palette built from a client's brand colours defines the same six roles or it is not a palette. It is a pile of hex. A `design-md` delivery earns those roles only after provenance and inline gates are present.
178: 
179: ---
180: 
181: ## 4. THE RULES
182: 
183: **One system per delivery.** A file, or a set of sibling charts shipped together, locks one system. When one chart in the set cannot be expressed in it, the whole set changes system or goes neutral. Recolouring the one exception is what makes a deck look assembled from parts. A `design-md` delivery is one such locked system: both palette blocks carry the same provenance and both clear the gates.
184: 
185: **Capacity is a ceiling, not a suggestion.** Four unordered categories is comfortable and five is not offered. A request for eleven categories is answered with the neutral system and labels, or by merging the tail before drawing. The ceiling lives in the palette file as the length of the series array, so an agent cannot reach a fifth slot without editing the source and failing the check.
186: 
187: **Derive light and dark, never introduce a hue.** A lighter value comes from mixing the chosen colour toward `surface`. A darker one comes from mixing it toward `ink`. Borrowing a value from another system to fill a gap breaks the encoding, because the borrowed value carries the other system's meaning. Every value shipped here was derived that way, inside one theme.
188: 
189: **A design-md delivery reads local values only.** `scripts/apply-design-md.cjs` parses the v3
190: `DESIGN.md` headings and columns, maps its background, text and chromatic rows into the shared
191: roles, and keeps the measured face before the substitute stack. It never fetches a site or copies a
192: remote resource. If the table cannot supply four chromatic values that clear the series gates, the
193: script names the shortfall and writes nothing.
194: 
195: ## Where the values come from
196: 
197: Since v0.18.0.0 the stock values are the evilcharts Style Reference: a white ground with a near-black
198: ink, a warmed near-black ground for dark, one flame hue that carries every first series, and a grey
199: ladder behind it. The packet carries its own copy at `assets/style-reference/evilcharts/`, the only
200: reference it ships, so the values here are derived from a file this packet owns rather than from one
201: a sibling library regenerates. `assets/style-reference/evilcharts/origin.md` records where the copy
202: came from and pins each file by hash. An earlier stock palette was derived from a different
203: reference; that copy is gone, and `--default` themes from this one.
204: 
205: **Since v0.13.0.0 the derivation is held rather than described.** The palette source carries a
206: `derivation` block naming the reference, its hash, the four departures with the gate each was made
207: to clear, and the values that come from an arithmetic the reference cannot carry: the ordered ramp's
208: interior rungs, spaced by equal contrast, and the dark rule, which is ink at alpha. The
209: `palette-derivation` family checks all of it — that the reference is still the file the palette was
210: derived from, that every value is either published by it, a named departure or one of those
211: arithmetic ones, and that each departure is still necessary and still sufficient. The prose above
212: stays because it explains why; the block is what fails when the two drift. The reference's
213: background, foreground, muted foreground and border carry the chrome on each ground; its flame
214: `--chart-1` carries the first series of every system; its greys carry the steps behind it in
215: `neutral`; its four chart hues carry `categorical`; and flame drawn toward each ground carries the
216: `ordered` ramp. Two values depart, each by the least amount that clears the mark gate, and the
217: palette source names both: the fourth neutral step on white, from the reference's `#A1A1A1` ring
218: to `#8F8F8F`, and the fourth on ink, from its `#484848` ash to `#616161`. One value is chosen
219: rather than derived: the dark ground is the reference's `#090909` warmed and lifted to `#141110`,
220: by the smallest amount that stops it reading as black, and every dark gate was recomputed against
221: it. The corner ladder takes the reference's 4.4px corner for track, swatch and pill and its 8.4px
222: card corner for the card; the 2px mark corner is the corpus's own. Everything else is verbatim.
223: 
224: **A theme boundary is the one place a hue may be re-chosen.** That rule above was written when there was one ground, and mixing toward the surface is exactly what makes a mark disappear when the surface is near-black. So a system's dark values are gated against the dark ground rather than derived from its light ones. A value that clears the dark gates ships unchanged on both grounds, which is what every categorical hue and the shared neutral grey do; only a value that fails them is re-chosen, at a hue the dark ground can carry and at whatever lightness clears the gate, and the palette source names each such move as a departure. Ratio parity between the grounds is not a rule and the shipped values do not have it.
225: 
226: The reason a hue may have to move is arithmetic rather than taste. A hue reaches its own ceiling of lightness: pure blue tops out near a tenth of the luminance pure yellow reaches, so a hue carrying the brightest slot on paper cannot always carry the brightest slot on ink without desaturating. Where that bites, the hue lands in the slot whose lightness it can reach with its chroma intact.
227: 
228: **The palette that ships needs none of it, and that is worth stating rather than leaving the rule to imply otherwise.** All four `categorical` hues clear the mark gate on both grounds unchanged, so the dark set is the light set: flame at 3.60:1 on white and 5.22:1 on the dark ground, teal at 3.67 and 5.12, violet at 4.12 and 4.56, rose at 3.75 and 5.01. The rotation rule stays because it is what a future reference with a narrower hue would need; this one does not exercise it.
229: 
230: Two systems would not rotate in any case. The `neutral` system has no hue to move, so its dark values are the same warm greys ordered from the other end. The `ordered` ramp stays in the ember family on both grounds, because a magnitude ramp needs one hue; what changes is direction, running toward the paper on light and toward the ink on dark.
231: 
232: **Index 0 is always the value furthest from that theme's ground.** On paper the first series value is the darkest and on ink it is the brightest, and in both cases it is the one that carries most. That is what keeps `neutral` ranking importance the same way on both grounds and keeps `ordered` reading as more in the same direction. A dark ramp that simply reversed the light array would satisfy the gates and still be wrong, because the light ramp's chroma was placed for a light ground.
233: 
234: **A figure never spends its data marks on the ink.** The first series of every system carries the
235: reading and takes a hue. Drawing the readings in the ink and reserving the one colour for the mark
236: the headline is about inverts what colour is for: it hands the accent to the exception and leaves
237: the subject in the same tone as the axis labels around it. The ranked system takes the ink as its
238: emphasis instead, so a plot reads as coloured marks with one that is not, rather than as plain
239: marks with one that is.
240: 
241: **The emphasis is spent once per form.** It is the value that says which mark the sentence is
242: about, so a form that marks two marks has either two findings or no emphasis. It also has a size:
243: the marked mark tends to be the largest one, and two of them put more than half a figure's ink in
244: the colour reserved for the exception — which is the inversion above arriving by a different route.
245: When the sentence genuinely has two subjects, the repair is the sentence, not a second mark. The
246: `emphasis-budget` family holds it in both directions: more than one marked row fails, and a lead
247: rule in the styles that no row reaches fails too, because a colour defined and never painted is a
248: decision nobody made.
249: 
250: **A single-series Cartesian form starts on the first series token of its own system.** A line, bar
251: or area with one data stream uses `--chart-series-1` for its primary mark, whichever system the
252: form declares; a neutral form stays neutral rather than borrowing the categorical ramp, because the
253: categorical emphasis token is ink and the orange highlighted mark would be lost. The `--chart-emphasis` role remains for the one highlighted mark the headline is
254: about. This keeps a lone series inside the same series vocabulary that a multi-series form
255: will use later, while the emphasis still reads as a deliberate exception. Unit grids, rings,
256: ordered ramps and other non-Cartesian forms keep their existing colour logic; their colour is
257: encoding a part-to-whole, magnitude or structural question rather than a lone Cartesian stream.
258: 
259: The rule is the HTML corpus' projection of the frozen shadcn examples: line and area examples
260: paint through a named series token (`chart-line-default.tsx:68-73`, `chart-area-default.tsx:70-76`),
261: and custom dots reserve their separate treatment for an active or deliberately named point
262: (`chart-line-label-custom.tsx:87-97`).
263: 
264: **Shapes that touch are separated by a stroke in `surface`.** Stacked segments, pie slices and treemap cells all carry a surface-coloured separator, so no two data colours ever share an edge. This is what makes the contrast gate satisfiable: with the separator, every mark is read against the ground rather than against its neighbour. Without it, four categories on a light ground is arithmetically impossible, because all-pairs separation at 3:1 runs out of room after two values.
265: 
266: **Colour is never the only cue.** Categories keep labels, ordered data keeps position or length, emphasis keeps a headline. Remove the colour and the chart still has to be readable. That is an accessibility floor and it is also a hedge against a reader printing in greyscale.
267: 
268: **A single mark may sweep along its own ramp, and only where the system already encodes magnitude.** A sweep restates an ordering the data already has, which is why it is honest on an `ordered` system and dishonest anywhere else. On a `neutral` or a `categorical` series the same sweep invents an ordering the data does not have, so it is refused there. That permits it on `calendar-grid`, `heat-matrix` and `progress-single`, and forbids it on the other eighteen forms.
269: 
270: The rule is written to be testable rather than judged. A gradient whose stops name two different
271: series values is a sweep, and it may appear only in a file whose declared system is `ordered`. A
272: gradient whose stops name one series value at two opacities is a fade rather than a sweep, which
273: is what the area under the line in `daily-line` already is, and the rule leaves it alone.
274: 
275: Permission is not obligation, and two of the three permitted forms have nothing to sweep. A
276: calendar cell and a matrix cell each carry one value, so a gradient across one of them would
277: show a variation inside a single reading. Only `progress-single` draws a mark whose length is
278: the magnitude, so only `progress-single` carries the sweep. Its ramp is anchored to the whole
279: track rather than to the fill, which is what makes the shade at the bar's end mean how far along
280: the goal it is rather than simply the end of the bar. It runs from the fourth step to the first,
281: leaving out the step nearest the ground, because that step reads at 1.76:1 and a bar that starts
282: invisible against its own track is a bar that starts in the wrong place.
283: 
284: A gradient reference is not a colour and cannot be typed into a `fill`. It reaches the mark
285: through a custom property, the way every other value in a template does.
286: 
287: ---
288: 
289: ## 5. THE CONTRAST GATES
290: 
291: These are computed from the palette file on every run, never restated in a test. A test that copies the values goes stale the first time somebody edits a colour.
292: 
293: Every gate runs twice, once per theme, against that theme's own surface. A stock run prints the two
294: as separate lines, `palette-source` and `palette-source-dark`; a design-md run adds `design-md` lines
295: for each delivery block. Nobody reads one theme's pass as covering both. A value that clears on
296: paper has proved nothing about ink.
297: 
298: | Gate | Threshold | Applies to, on either ground |
299: | --- | --- | --- |
300: | `textOnSurface` | 4.5:1 | `ink` and `muted` against that theme's `surface` |
301: | `markOnSurface` | 3.0:1 | Every series value in an `importance` or `category` system, and every emphasis value |
302: | `rampDarkestOnSurface` | 3.0:1 | The step of a `magnitude` system furthest from the ground, which is the darkest on paper and the brightest on ink |
303: | `rampLightestOnSurface` | 1.15:1 | The step nearest the ground, so a low cell is distinguishable from an empty one |
304: | `rampStepSeparation` | 1.3:1 | Adjacent steps of a `magnitude` system |
305: | `emphasisAgainstFirstSeries` | 1.5:1 | Emphasis against `series-1` |
306: 
307: The design-md adapter applies `textOnSurface` to ink and muted, `markOnSurface` to all four series
308: and emphasis, and `emphasisAgainstFirstSeries` to emphasis; the corpus check then holds a delivery's
309: blocks to that set plus the series separation, comparing every pair of series rather than adjacent
310: values alone, with a pair passing on the ratio or on thirty degrees of hue. The two ramp-end gates
311: belong to the stock magnitude systems, and the adapter does not apply them. The rule role remains
312: deliberately ungated, but the dark rule still has to be the dark ink colour at a non-full alpha.
313: 
314: Two of those names were written when there was one ground and now read wrong on the other: on ink
315: the step this table calls the darkest is the brightest one. The check tests the end by its distance
316: from the ground rather than by its position in the array, and it says which end it tested in the
317: failure it prints.
318: 
319: The rename stays a proposal, and the reason has changed since it was first written. It is now a
320: scoping fact rather than a judgement: `rampDarkestOnSurface` and `rampLightestOnSurface` reach
321: three files, being this document, the palette source and the check that reads the keys by name,
322: and the check is the one file the phase that would rename them is not allowed to touch. Renaming
323: here and not there would leave a gate reading a key nobody defines, which is a worse state than
324: two badly named keys that work. `rampFarEndOnSurface` and `rampNearEndOnSurface` are the names
325: the rename should land under, and it lands as one edit across all three files or not at all.
326: 
327: ### Which end of a ramp the gates hold
328: 
329: A ramp's array runs from the value furthest from the ground to the value nearest it, and the check
330: asserts that ordering before it gates either end. That is what stops a reversed array from passing:
331: reversal keeps every step separation intact, so a check that gated whichever end happened to be
332: lighter would accept a ramp that now reads backwards.
333: 
334: ### Why a ramp is gated differently
335: 
336: A ramp step is read as part of a group, against its legend and its neighbours. An individual mark is read alone. Requiring 3:1 of every ramp step would delete the light end of every sequential scale, which is the half that encodes "low", so the gate holds the dark end and the step separation instead.
337: 
338: ### The one role deliberately not gated
339: 
340: `rule` is ungated, and this is a decision rather than an oversight. A gridline pushed to 3:1 competes with the data drawn over it, and it carries no information a reader has to recover. Structure that fails to read is a design defect reviewed by eye. The exemption is written into the palette file next to the gates so nobody has to guess whether it was intended.
341: 
342: ---
343: 
344: ## 6. WHAT IS ENFORCED AND WHAT IS NOT
345: 
346: Enforced by `scripts/check-corpus.cjs`, on every run:
347: 
348: - Every gate in the table above, computed from the palette file, once per theme against that theme's own surface. That holds for the three stock systems the palette file describes; the design-md adapter applies the subset named under the table, in `scripts/apply-design-md.cjs` at write time and again over a delivery's own blocks in the corpus check.
349: - Every system defines as many series values as its declared capacity, on both grounds.
350: - A `magnitude` system runs from the step furthest from the ground to the step nearest it, without reversing.
351: - The dark `rule` value is that theme's ink at an alpha, rather than a solid grey that a card edge would have to sit over.
352: - Each of a template's palette blocks matches the palette file exactly, in both directions, and no file carries more than one block per theme.
353: - A `design-md` block carries a first-line provenance comment with a well-formed 64-hex hash, and its inline values clear the same gates on both grounds.
354: - No colour literal appears anywhere outside a palette block.
355: - No corner value appears anywhere outside a palette block: a stylesheet corner resolves through a rung, and the drawing code computes a corner rather than typing one.
356: - An indexed data class carries the palette token of its own index, the indices run from one without a gap, and they stop at the declared system's capacity. `series-mapping` is the only rule that reads the mapping itself rather than the values on either side of it, and it is the rule a reversed or shuffled encoding fails. Everything else on this list passes a file whose classes hand the tokens out in the wrong order, because every other rule asks where a value came from and none asks which mark received it.
357: 
358: The sweep rule was the last entry on this list and it has moved up onto it. `gradient-sweep`
359: resolves each gradient's stops through the classes that carry them, counts the distinct series
360: values it finds and fails a gradient naming two of them in a file whose declared system is not
361: `ordered`. A gradient naming one series value at two opacities is a fade and is left alone,
362: which is what keeps the area under a line untouched.
363: 
364: Advisory, and reviewed by a person:
365: 
366: - Whether the gridline weight looks right at the size the chart ships.
367: - Whether two categorical hues that both clear the gate are still easy to tell apart. Their luminances are spread so the set survives greyscale, and that is a design property rather than a measurable one.
368: - Whether a sweep reads as one mark deepening rather than as two marks. That is the judgement the rule cannot make, and the reason the rule is a ceiling on where a sweep may appear rather than an instruction to use one.
369: 
370: The split is deliberate. A rule the tooling does not check describes the author's intentions rather than the artifact, so anything stated as binding above is checked, and anything that cannot be checked is named here as advice.
371: 
372: ---
373: 
374: ## 7. WHY THREE BUILT-IN SYSTEMS AND ONE ADAPTER
375: 
376: A fourth semantic system of "neutral with one accent colour" was considered and cut. Emphasis is a
377: role that every built-in system already carries, so a system whose only difference is that the role
378: is filled adds a name without adding an answer. In `neutral` the emphasis value is the only
379: chromatic colour in the palette, which is exactly what that fourth semantic system would have
380: delivered, reached by filling a role instead of by switching system.
381: 
382: `design-md` is not that system. It is an adapter for a measured local style reference: it changes
383: the values that fill the shared roles, records the source hash, and passes the same gates. It does
384: not add a new meaning to colour, a new capacity or a new chart form. The cost of keeping that
385: adapter separate is one more checker branch; the benefit is that stock source equality remains
386: strict and a themed delivery can be traced without putting client colours into the stock palette.
387: 
388: The emphasis role is required in all three built-in systems and in the adapter. A system where
389: emphasis is undefined has no way to express the most common request in the corpus: this one bar is
390: the point.
391: 
392: ---
393: 
394: ## 8. WHAT IS DELIBERATELY ABSENT
395: 
396: Two things a reader coming from a charting library will look for and not find. Both were
397: considered and both are cut, for the same reason section 7 cuts a fourth system: a name
398: that adds no answer costs more than the gap it fills.
399: 
400: ### A diverging system
401: 
402: A diverging ramp encodes distance from a meaningful midpoint, and it earns its place when a
403: form reads two directions away from zero on one continuous scale. No form in the corpus
404: does. `heat-matrix` and `calendar-grid` both run one direction from low to high, which is
405: what `ordered` already encodes, and `waterfall` separates rises from falls by category
406: rather than by magnitude, which is what `categorical` already encodes. Adding the system
407: now would mean shipping a scale with no consumer and letting an author reach for it because
408: it exists.
409: 
410: What would reopen it is a catalog form that genuinely needs a midpoint: a matrix of signed
411: change, a variance-against-plan grid, a correlation table. When such a form arrives, the
412: system arrives with it, and the two are added together so the scale has a consumer on the
413: day it ships.
414: 
415: ### Pattern fills
416: 
417: Hatching or dotting a mark so that colour is not the only cue is a real technique, and this
418: corpus does not need it. The rule above already forbids colour carrying meaning alone, and
419: every form satisfies it another way: a stacked segment carries its value in the segment, a
420: ring group carries its count beside the label, a scatter point carries a hover title, a band
421: carries a legend swatch in the same order as the stack. The luminances in each system are
422: spread so the set survives greyscale, which is the printing case patterns are usually
423: reached for.
424: 
425: The cost of adding them is not small. A pattern changes the visual register of every chart
426: it appears in, so it is either corpus-wide, which redraws the whole product for a problem
427: none of these forms has, or per-form, which makes two charts in one deck look like they came
428: from different tools. If a future form does encode something in colour alone and cannot
429: label it, that form carries the pattern, and this paragraph is the reason nothing else does.
430: 
431: ---

682: ## 5. CONVERTING LOGIC TO EXECUTABLE CODE
683: 
684: ### When to Extract Logic from Markdown
685: 
686: **Purpose**: Separate documentation from executable code for better maintainability, testability, and reusability.
687: 
688: **Decision Criteria**:
689: 
690: | Pattern Type          | Keep in Markdown  | Extract to Code           | Reasoning                                    |
691: | --------------------- | ----------------- | ------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
692: | **Python functions**  | ❌ No              | ✅ Yes → `/scripts/*.py`   | Type safety, unit testing, reusability       |
693: | **YAML configs**      | ❌ No              | ✅ Yes → `/assets/*.yaml`  | Dynamic loading, version control, validation |
694: | **Decision trees**    | ⚠️ High-level only | ✅ Details → YAML + Python | Machine-readable, can be validated           |
695: | **Command mappings**  | ⚠️ Examples only   | ✅ Full map → YAML         | Easier maintenance, can be imported          |
696: | **Workflow diagrams** | ✅ Yes (generated) | ✅ Source → YAML           | YAML = source of truth, diagram = output     |
697: | **Checklists**        | ✅ Yes             | ❌ No                      | Human-readable is primary use case           |
698: | **Before/after code** | ✅ Yes             | ❌ No                      | Educational, not executable                  |
699: 
700: ### Extraction Pattern
701: 
702: **In Markdown (Reference File)**:
703: ```markdown
704: ### [Workflow Name]
705: 
706: [High-level description of what the workflow does]
707: 
708: **Implementation:** See [workflow_name.py](../scripts/workflow_name.py) for execution logic and [workflow-config.yaml](../assets/workflow-config.yaml) for configuration.
709: 
710: **Quick Overview**:
711: 1. [Step 1 - high level]
712: 2. [Step 2 - high level]
713: 3. [Step 3 - high level]
714: 
715: **Configuration Options:**
716: - See YAML config for customizable parameters
717: - Default values optimized for common use cases
718: ```
719: 
720: ### Benefits of Separation
721: 
722: - **Type safety** - Python type hints catch errors at development time
723: - **Testability** - Unit tests for logic, integration tests for workflows
724: - **Reusability** - Imported by multiple skills or scripts
725: - **Version control** - Git diffs show logic changes clearly
726: - **Schema validation** - YAML can be validated against schemas
727: - **Dynamic loading** - Configuration changes without code edits
728: 
729: ### Example: Mode Detection Extraction
730: 
731: **❌ BEFORE** (inline Python in markdown):
732: \```python
733: def detect_mode(request):
734:     if '$quick' in request: return 'quick', 5
735:     elif '$ticket' in request: return 'ticket', 10
736:     return 'interactive', 10
737: \```
738: 
739: **✅ AFTER** (extracted with type safety):
740: 
741: `/scripts/mode_detection.py`:
742: \```python
743: from dataclasses import dataclass
744: 
745: @dataclass
746: class ModeConfig:
747:     mode: str
748:     depth_rounds: int
749: 
750: def detect_mode(request: str) -> ModeConfig:
751:     """Detect mode from command shortcuts."""
752:     if '$quick' in request:
753:         return ModeConfig('quick', 5)
754:     elif '$ticket' in request:
755:         return ModeConfig('ticket', 10)
756:     return ModeConfig('interactive', 10)
757: \```
758: 
759: `/tests/test_mode_detection.py`:
760: \```python
761: def test_quick_mode():
762:     assert detect_mode("$quick fix").mode == 'quick'
763: \```
764: 
765: **Why better:** Type hints, testable, reusable, separated from docs
766:

769: ## 6. YAML CONFIGURATION PATTERNS
770: 
771: ### Purpose
772: 
773: **YAML for configuration data** - Separate configuration from documentation for easier maintenance and dynamic loading.
774: 
775: **When to use YAML**:
776: - Configuration data (thresholds, mappings, rules)
777: - Data structures (nested objects, lists)
778: - Workflow definitions (step sequences, pipelines)
779: - Decision trees (conditional logic patterns)
780: - Validation schemas
781: 
782: ### Standard YAML Structure
783: 
784: ```yaml
785: # [config-name].yaml
786: metadata:
787:   version: "1.0.0"
788:   description: "Configuration for [feature name]"
789: 
790: config:
791:   threshold_values:
792:     low: 1
793:     medium: 5
794:     high: 10
795:   feature_flags:
796:     enable_feature_x: true
797:   mappings:
798:     $quick: "quick_mode"
799:     $ticket: "ticket_mode"
800: ```
801: 
802: ### File Organization
803: 
804: ```
805: .skilled/skills/[skill-name]/
806: ├── assets/
807: │   ├── workflow-configs/
808: │   │   ├── canvas-methodology.yaml
809: │   │   ├── variant-detection.yaml
810: │   │   └── complexity-scoring.yaml
811: │   ├── mappings/
812: │   │   ├── command-mappings.yaml
813: │   │   ├── mode-recognition.yaml
814: │   │   └── shortcut-definitions.yaml
815: │   └── templates/
816: │       └── [template files]
817: ```
818: 
819: ### Loading Pattern (Python)
820: 
821: ```python
822: import yaml
823: from pathlib import Path
824: 
825: def load_config(config_name: str) -> dict:
826:     """Load YAML config from assets directory."""
827:     config_path = Path(__file__).parent.parent / f"assets/{config_name}.yaml"
828:     with open(config_path) as f:
829:         return yaml.safe_load(f)['config']
830: 
831: # Usage
832: config = load_config("canvas-methodology")
833: ```
834: 
835: ### Example: Variant Detection Rules
836: 
837: **❌ BEFORE** (markdown table):
838: ```markdown
839: | Trigger                    | Action             |
840: | -------------------------- | ------------------ |
841: | "show options"             | Offer 3-5 variants |
842: | Complexity 7+ + "not sure" | Offer variants     |
843: ```
844: 
845: **✅ AFTER** (YAML + Python):
846: 
847: `/assets/variant-detection-rules.yaml`:
848: ```yaml
849: config:
850:   variant_triggers:
851:     explicit_keywords: ["show me options", "variations"]
852:     implicit:
853:       complexity_threshold: 7
854:       uncertainty_signals: ["not sure", "what would work"]
855:   variant_count:
856:     simple: [2, 3]
857:     complex: [5, 10]
858: ```
859: 
860: `/scripts/variant_detector.py`:
861: ```python
862: import yaml
863: 
864: class VariantDetector:
865:     def __init__(self, config_path: str):
866:         with open(config_path) as f:
867:             self.config = yaml.safe_load(f)['config']
868: 
869:     def should_generate_variants(self, request: str, complexity: int) -> bool:
870:         keywords = self.config['variant_triggers']['explicit_keywords']
871:         if any(kw in request.lower() for kw in keywords):
872:             return True
873: 
874:         threshold = self.config['variant_triggers']['implicit']['complexity_threshold']
875:         if complexity >= threshold:
876:             signals = self.config['variant_triggers']['implicit']['uncertainty_signals']
877:             return any(s in request.lower() for s in signals)
878:         return False
879: ```
880: 
881: **Why better:** Dynamic config loading, easier maintenance, schema validation possible

885: ## 7. PYTHON SCRIPT INTEGRATION
886: 
887: ### When to Use Python for Logic
888: 
889: **Use Python scripts when**:
890: - Procedural logic (workflows, algorithms)
891: - Complex conditionals (multi-step decisions)
892: - Data transformation (processing, validation)
893: - API integration (external services)
894: - File operations (reading, parsing, generating)
895: 
896: ### Type Hints and Docstring Standards
897: 
898: **Always include**:
899: - Type hints for parameters and return values
900: - Google-style docstrings (Args, Returns, Raises, Examples)
901: - Dataclasses for structured data
902: 
903: **Example**:
904: ```python
905: from dataclasses import dataclass
906: from pathlib import Path
907: 
908: @dataclass
909: class ValidationResult:
910:     is_valid: bool
911:     errors: list[str]
912: 
913: def validate_config(config_path: Path) -> ValidationResult:
914:     """
915:     Validate configuration file.
916: 
917:     Args:
918:         config_path: Path to YAML config file
919: 
920:     Returns:
921:         ValidationResult with status and errors
922: 
923:     Raises:
924:         FileNotFoundError: If config doesn't exist
925:     """
926:     if not config_path.exists():
927:         raise FileNotFoundError(f"Config not found: {config_path}")
928:     # Validation logic
929:     return ValidationResult(is_valid=True, errors=[])
930: ```
931: 
932: ### Unit Testing Requirements
933: 
934: **Every Python script must have tests**:
935: - Naming: `test_[script_name].py` in `/tests/` directory
936: - Coverage: ≥80% line coverage
937: - Framework: pytest
938: 
939: **Example**:
940: ```python
941: import pytest
942: from scripts.config_validator import validate_config
943: 
944: def test_validate_success(tmp_path):
945:     config = tmp_path / "config.yaml"
946:     config.write_text("config:\n  threshold: 5")
947:     result = validate_config(config)
948:     assert result.is_valid
949: 
950: def test_validate_missing_file():
951:     with pytest.raises(FileNotFoundError):
952:         validate_config(Path("nonexistent.yaml"))
953: ```
954: 
955: ### Import and Reference Patterns
956: 
957: **Python import order**: Standard library → Third-party → Local
958: 
959: **Markdown references**:
960: ```markdown
961: **See also:** [script_name.py](../scripts/script_name.py), [config.yaml](../assets/config.yaml)
962: ```
963: 
964: ### Example: Workflow Decision Logic
965: 
966: **❌ BEFORE** (text decision tree):
967: ```markdown
968: IF "$quick": use quick mode (5 rounds)
969: IF "$ticket": use ticket mode (10 rounds)
970: OTHERWISE: use interactive mode
971: ```
972: 
973: **✅ AFTER** (Python with type safety):
974: 
975: `/scripts/workflow_router.py`:
976: ```python
977: from typing import Literal
978: from dataclasses import dataclass
979: 
980: WorkflowMode = Literal["quick", "ticket", "interactive"]
981: 
982: @dataclass
983: class WorkflowDecision:
984:     mode: WorkflowMode
985:     depth_rounds: int
986: 
987: def route_workflow(request: str) -> WorkflowDecision:
988:     """Route request to appropriate workflow."""
989:     if '$quick' in request.lower():
990:         return WorkflowDecision("quick", 5)
991:     if '$ticket' in request.lower():
992:         return WorkflowDecision("ticket", 10)
993:     return WorkflowDecision("interactive", 10)
994: ```
995: 
996: `/tests/test_workflow_router.py`:
997: ```python
998: def test_quick_mode():
999:     assert route_workflow("$quick fix").mode == "quick"
1000: 
1001: def test_default_mode():
1002:     assert route_workflow("help me").mode == "interactive"
1003: ```
1004: 
1005: **Why better:** Type-safe with Literal, testable, structured with dataclass
1006: 
1007: ---
1008: 
1009: ## 8. STANDARD STRUCTURE TEMPLATE
1010: 
1011: ### Complete Skill Directory Structure
1012: 
1013: **Path:** `.skilled/skills/` (singular, not `skills` or `openskills`)
1014: 
1015: ```
1016: .skilled/skills/[skill-name]/
1017: ├── SKILL.md                    # Main skill file (Level 2 in progressive disclosure)
1018: ├── references/                 # Deep-dive technical documentation (Level 3)
1019: │   ├── workflow-name.md        # Multi-phase workflows with checkpoints (kebab-case)
1020: │   ├── patterns-library.md     # Before/after code patterns (kebab-case)
1021: │   ├── debugging-guide.md      # Systematic troubleshooting (kebab-case)
1022: │   └── quick-reference.md      # Commands, shortcuts, checklists (kebab-case)
1023: ├── scripts/                    # Executable Python logic
1024: │   ├── mode_detection.py       # Procedural logic, algorithms
1025: │   ├── workflow_router.py      # Decision logic
1026: │   ├── config_validator.py     # Data transformation
1027: │   └── __init__.py             # Package initialization
1028: ├── assets/                     # Configuration and data files
1029: │   ├── workflow-configs/       # YAML workflow definitions
1030: │   │   ├── canvas-methodology.yaml
1031: │   │   └── complexity-scoring.yaml
1032: │   ├── mappings/               # YAML mapping data
1033: │   │   ├── command-mappings.yaml
1034: │   │   └── mode-recognition.yaml
1035: │   └── templates/              # Markdown/code templates
1036: │       ├── template-name.md
1037: │       └── component-template.tsx
1038: └── tests/                      # Unit and integration tests
1039:     ├── test_mode_detection.py
1040:     ├── test_workflow_router.py
1041:     ├── test_config_validator.py
1042:     └── __init__.py
1043: ```
1044: 
1045: ### Directory Purposes
1046: 
1047: **SKILL.md** (Required): Overview, workflow (3-5 steps), rules. Target: <200 lines
1048: 
1049: **references/** (Optional): Detailed workflows, patterns, debugging. Target: 500-3000 lines/file. **All authored filenames must use kebab-case.**
1050: 
1051: **scripts/** (Optional): Python logic - procedural, routing, validation. Requires type hints, tests
1052: 
1053: **assets/** (Optional): YAML configs, workflow definitions, templates, mappings
1054: 
1055: **tests/** (Required if scripts/ exists): Unit tests with ≥80% coverage, pytest, `test_[name].py`
1056: 
1057: ### When to Create Each Directory
1058: 
1059: | Directory     | Create When                                                     | Don't Create When                           |
1060: | ------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
1061: | `references/` | Content >200 lines, multi-phase workflows, systematic debugging | Simple skills <200 lines total              |
1062: | `scripts/`    | Python logic extracted from markdown, reusable functions        | Pure documentation, no executable logic     |
1063: | `assets/`     | YAML configs, templates, structured data                        | No configuration data, inline examples only |
1064: | `tests/`      | `scripts/` directory exists                                     | No Python scripts to test                   |
1065: 
1066: ### Integration Pattern
1067: 
1068: **How components work together:**
1069: - SKILL.md references scripts: `[workflow_router.py](./scripts/workflow_router.py)`
1070: - Scripts load configs: `yaml.safe_load(f"../assets/config.yaml")`
1071: - Tests verify scripts: `assert route_workflow("input").mode == "expected"`
1072: - Markdown links to all: "See [script.py](../scripts/), [config.yaml](../assets/)"
1073: 
1074: ---
1075:

14: # Skill Reference File Templates - AI Agent Skills
15: 
16: Templates for creating reference files in AI agent skills with deep-dive technical guidance.
17: 
18: ---
19: 
20: ## 1. OVERVIEW
21: 
22: ### Location & Naming
23: 
24: **Location:** `.skilled/skills/[skill-name]/references/`
25: 
26: **Naming Convention:** kebab-case with `.md` extension only
27: 
28: | ✅ Valid Names | ❌ Invalid Names |
29: |---------------|-----------------|
30: | `implementation-workflows.md` | `ImplementationWorkflows.md` (PascalCase) |
31: | `tool-catalog.md` | `tool_catalog.md` (snake_case) |
32: | `debugging-guide.md` | `DebuggingGuide.MD` (wrong case) |
33: | `quick-reference.md` | `quickReference.md` (camelCase) |
34: | `code-quality-standards.md` | `code quality standards.md` (spaces) |
35: 
36: ---
37: 
38: ## 2. DOCUMENT STRUCTURE
39: 
40: ### Document Structure: Title and Intro
41: 
42: **CRITICAL: The intro after the H1 title must be 1-2 SHORT sentences only.**
43: 
44: ```markdown
45: ---
46: title: [Title]
47: description: [One-line description - same as intro]
48: trigger_phrases:
49:   - "[distinctive phrase one]"
50:   - "[distinctive phrase two]"
51:   - "[distinctive phrase three]"
52: importance_tier: normal
53: contextType: general
54: version: 1.0.0.0
55: ---
56: 
57: # [Title]
58: 
59: [1-2 SHORT sentences only. Brief hook/summary. NO subsections, NO headers here.]
60: 
61: ---
62: 
63: \## 1. OVERVIEW
64: [All detailed content goes here, NOT in the intro]
65: 
66: ```
67: 
68: Every reference file carries this full 5-field frontmatter block: the Skill Advisor harvests it as routing signal (3-8 lowercase multi-word `trigger_phrases` drawn from the doc's content. `importance_tier` defaults to `normal`, with `important` only for formal contract docs. `contextType` is one of `planning|research|implementation|general`). See [frontmatter-templates.md](../../../sk-create-frontmatter/assets/frontmatter-templates.md) for field rules.
69: 
70: > **WARNING: DO NOT duplicate content between intro and Section 1.**
71: > The intro is a hook. Section 1 provides the details.
72: 
73: #### GOOD Intro Structure
74: 
75: ```markdown
76: # Git Commit Workflows
77: 
78: This reference turns a mixed working tree into a small set of reviewable commits.
79: 
80: ---
81: 
82: \## 1. OVERVIEW
83: 
84: ### Purpose
85: Each rule keeps one commit focused on one intent, so history stays easy to read, review and revert.
86: 
87: ### When to Use
88: - Creating commits with multiple file changes
89: - Filtering generated files from commits
90: - Writing clear commit messages
91: 
92: ### Core Principle
93: Atomic commits with clear intent + filtered artifacts = maintainable Git history.
94: ```
95: 
96: #### BAD Intro Structure (duplicates content)
97: 
98: ```markdown
99: # Git Commit Workflows
100: 
101: Step-by-step workflows for creating clean, atomic commits with proper filtering.
102: 
103: ### Core Principle   ← WRONG: No headers in intro!
104: Atomic commits with clear intent + filtered artifacts = maintainable Git history.
105: 
106: ### When to Use      ← WRONG: This belongs in Section 1!
107: - Creating commits with multiple file changes
108: 
109: ---
110: 
111: \## 1. OVERVIEW
112: 
113: ### Purpose
114: Provides systematic workflows...  ← Now this duplicates the intro!
115: 
116: ### Core Principle
117: Atomic commits...  ← DUPLICATED from intro!
118: ```
119: 
120: #### Intro vs Section 1 Content Placement
121: 
122: | Content Type          | Intro (after H1) | Section 1 OVERVIEW |
123: | --------------------- | ---------------- | ------------------ |
124: | 1-2 sentence summary  | ✅ YES            | ❌ NO (don't repeat) |
125: | Core Principle        | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES              |
126: | When to Use           | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES              |
127: | Primary Sources       | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (as "Key Sources") |
128: | Purpose (detailed)    | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES              |
129: | Prerequisites         | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES              |
130: | Any H3 subsections    | ❌ NEVER          | ✅ YES              |
131: 
132: ---
133: 
134: ### Reference Body Skeleton
135: 
136: **Every reference body follows this order.** The hook and the Purpose say different things: the hook names the job, and the Purpose names the outcome.
137: 
138: ```markdown
139: # [Title]
140: 
141: [1-2 sentence hook: what this reference covers and when to reach for it.]
142: 
143: ---
144: 
145: ## 1. OVERVIEW
146: 
147: ### Purpose
148: 
149: [The outcome this reference produces, in one or two sentences.]
150: 
151: ### When to Use
152: 
153: - [Trigger that sends a reader here]
154: - [Second trigger]
155: 
156: ### Core Principle
157: 
158: [One-line statement that governs every rule below.]
159: 
160: ### Boundaries
161: 
162: - **In scope**: [What this reference owns]
163: - **Out of scope**: [What belongs in a sibling reference]
164: 
165: ### Key Sources
166: 
167: - [title](url) - [What the source establishes]
168: 
169: ---
170: 
171: ## 2. [CONTENT SECTION]
172: 
173: ### [Rule Group]
174: 
175: - **Rule:** [What to do]
176: - **Why:** [The failure it prevents]
177: - **Check:** [How to verify it]
178: 
179: ---
180: 
181: ## 3. [CONTENT SECTION]
182: 
183: [Body of the section]
184: 
185: ---
186: 
187: ## 4. RELATED RESOURCES
188: 
189: - [title](./sibling-reference.md) - [What the reader gets there]
190: ```
191: 
192: **Rules the skeleton encodes:**
193: - Core Principle, Boundaries and Key Sources follow Purpose and When to Use, in that order, and each appears only when it has content.
194: - Content sections use integer numbers only: `## 2.`, `## 3.`, and so on.
195: - Rule fields are `- **Label:** text` bullets, never two bold labels on consecutive lines.
196: - Links are `[title](url)`, never a bare URL.
197: - Every `---` has a blank line above it, so a divider never turns the line above into a setext heading.
198: - A related section, when present, is the last H2.
199:
